_comment: Master list of every usability concept AS92006 expects students to know. Each mini-game question refers to these by 'id'. See content/README.md for the full schema.

principles.plain_definition: The interface always shows the user what's currently happening, so they're never left guessing.
principles.exam_wording: The system should always keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within reasonable time.
principles.not_achieved_tip: Don't just describe the feature (e.g. 'there's a loading bar') - say that it works because it keeps the user informed about what the system is doing.

principles.name_en: Match Between System and the Real World
principles.plain_definition: The interface uses words, icons and ideas the user already understands from everyday life, instead of technical or system-based language.
principles.exam_wording: The system should speak the users' language, with words, phrases and concepts familiar to the user, following real-world conventions.
principles.not_achieved_tip: Naming a familiar icon isn't enough on its own - explain that it works because it matches something the user already recognises from the real world.

principles.plain_definition: Users can back out of a mistake or an unwanted action easily, such as with an undo button or a clear cancel option - it's their 'emergency exit'.
principles.exam_wording: Users often choose system functions by mistake and need a clearly marked emergency exit to leave the unwanted state without having to go through an extended process.
principles.not_achieved_tip: This is not the same as being able to roam around a site freely. It specifically means an escape route - undo, cancel, back - out of a mistake.

principles.plain_definition: Similar things look and behave the same way throughout the interface, and match what users expect from other software they've used.
principles.exam_wording: Users should not have to wonder whether different words, situations or actions mean the same thing; interfaces should follow platform and industry conventions.
principles.not_achieved_tip: Say whether it's internal (consistent within this one interface) or external (consistent with other apps/sites the user already knows) consistency, not just 'it's the same'.

principles.plain_definition: The design stops a mistake from happening in the first place, before the user even attempts it.
principles.exam_wording: Even better than good error messages is a careful design which prevents a problem from occurring in the first place, by eliminating error-prone conditions or presenting a confirmation option.
principles.not_achieved_tip: Error Prevention happens BEFORE a mistake. If the feature only appears after something has already gone wrong, that's Error Recovery, not Error Prevention.

principles.plain_definition: The user can see their options on screen instead of having to remember information from an earlier screen or from memory.
principles.exam_wording: Minimise the user's memory load by making objects, actions and options visible, so the user does not have to recall information from one part of the interface to another.
principles.not_achieved_tip: Link this to reducing what the user has to remember, not just 'it's easy to see'.

principles.plain_definition: The interface offers shortcuts or accelerators - like keyboard shortcuts or saved preferences - that let experienced users work faster, without getting in the way of new users.
principles.exam_wording: Accelerators - unseen by the novice user - may often speed up the interaction for the expert user, such that the system can cater to both inexperienced and experienced users.
principles.not_achieved_tip: This is about speeding up an expert user with shortcuts, not about giving any user an escape route out of a mistake - that's User Control and Freedom.

principles.plain_definition: Screens only show information that's relevant right now; extra detail is left out or tucked away so nothing distracts from the task.
principles.exam_wording: Interfaces should not contain information which is irrelevant or rarely needed, since every extra unit of information competes with the relevant units and diminishes their visibility.
principles.not_achieved_tip: Explain that removing clutter helps the user focus on their current task, not just that the screen 'looks clean'.

principles.name_en: Help Users Recognise, Diagnose, and Recover From Errors
principles.plain_definition: When something does go wrong, the interface tells the user in plain language what happened and how to fix it.
principles.exam_wording: Error messages should be expressed in plain language (no codes), precisely indicate the problem, and constructively suggest a solution.
principles.not_achieved_tip: This happens AFTER a mistake has already been made. If the feature stops the mistake from happening at all, that's Error Prevention, not this.

principles.plain_definition: Even though it's best if the system needs no explanation, help information is there when the user needs it, and it's easy to search and focused on their task.
principles.exam_wording: It may be necessary to provide help and documentation; such information should be easy to search, focused on the user's task, list concrete steps, and not be too large.
principles.not_achieved_tip: Say why the help is easy to find and use for this specific task, not just that 'there's a help page'.

principles.plain_definition: The interface can be used by people with a range of abilities, e.g. enough colour contrast, readable text sizes, or alt text for images.
principles.exam_wording: The interface should be usable by people with a range of abilities and needs, including visual, motor, hearing or cognitive differences.
principles.not_achieved_tip: Name the specific access need being supported (e.g. low vision, colour-blindness), not just 'it's accessible'.

principles.plain_definition: How much work the interface asks of the user should match how important or risky the task is - simple tasks should be quick, and serious tasks can reasonably ask for more care.
principles.exam_wording: The level of effort required from the user should be proportional to the significance or risk of the task being carried out.
principles.not_achieved_tip: Link the amount of effort asked of the user to the importance of that specific task, not just 'it takes a few steps'.

principles.plain_definition: Internal consistency means things behave the same way within one interface; external consistency means it behaves the way similar apps or sites already do.
principles.exam_wording: Internal consistency refers to uniformity within a single product; external consistency refers to alignment with conventions used across other products.
principles.not_achieved_tip: Be specific about which kind of consistency you mean - within this interface, or compared to other software the user already knows.

principles.plain_definition: A new user can figure out how to use the interface quickly, without much trial and error.
principles.exam_wording: The ease with which new users can accomplish basic tasks the first time they encounter the design.
principles.not_achieved_tip: Talk about how quickly a first-time user can work it out, not how much they'll like it.

principles.plain_definition: How much information the interface asks the user to hold in their head at once - too much, and they'll make mistakes or give up.
principles.exam_wording: The interface should minimise the load placed on a user's working memory during a task.
principles.not_achieved_tip: Explain what the user would otherwise have had to remember, and how the design reduces that.

principles.plain_definition: How quickly the interface reacts to what the user does - slow responses without feedback make users think something is broken.
principles.exam_wording: The interval between a user's action and the system's response, and the feedback given during that interval.
principles.not_achieved_tip: Say what would happen to the user's confidence if the response were slower, not just 'it's fast'.

principles.name_mi: Te Tika o te Tuhi i te Reo Māori
principles.plain_definition: Te reo Māori text on the interface is spelled correctly, including macrons (tohutō), so meaning isn't lost or changed.
principles.exam_wording: Accurate and clear use of te reo Māori, including correct orthography such as tohutō (macrons), supports usability and respects the language.
principles.not_achieved_tip: A missing or wrong tohutō can change a word's meaning entirely - explain what is wrong and why it matters for the user, not just that 'the spelling looks off'.

principles.plain_definition: The interface is welcoming, respectful and looks after its users, the way a good host looks after guests.
principles.exam_wording: Manaakitanga refers to hospitality, care and respect shown to users through the way an interface welcomes and supports them.
principles.not_achieved_tip: Explain how the specific feature makes a user feel welcomed or cared for, not just that the site 'looks nice'.

principles.plain_definition: Users have control and self-determination over the interface and their own information - they're in charge, not the system.
principles.exam_wording: Rangatiratanga refers to self-determination and authority; interfaces should give users genuine control over their choices, data and experience.
principles.not_achieved_tip: Link this to users having real control or authority over their own data or choices, not just to the site being easy to use.

principles.plain_definition: The interface supports relationships and connection, e.g. letting a user share their pepeha (waka, maunga, awa, iwi, hapū) or connect with a community.
principles.exam_wording: Whanaungatanga refers to relationships and connection; interfaces can support this through features that reflect whakapapa, community or shared identity.
principles.not_achieved_tip: Name the specific relationship or connection the feature supports (e.g. sharing pepeha), not just 'it feels friendly'.

principles.plain_definition: The interface shows respect for spiritual dimensions, such as acknowledging atua (deities) or tūpuna (ancestors) where relevant to the content.
principles.exam_wording: Wairuatanga refers to the spiritual dimension; interfaces can acknowledge atua and tūpuna appropriately where relevant to their content and audience.
principles.not_achieved_tip: Say specifically what spiritual element is (or isn't) being acknowledged, rather than describing the design generally.

principles.name_mi: Te Tautoko i te Whakaputa Mātauranga Māori
principles.plain_definition: The interface gives space for Māori knowledge, stories or practices to be shared in their own right, not squeezed into a format built for something else.
principles.exam_wording: The extent to which an interface's structure and features allow mātauranga Māori to be expressed appropriately, rather than forcing it into a format designed for other content.
principles.not_achieved_tip: Explain what about the layout or feature specifically allows (or blocks) mātauranga Māori being expressed properly.
